ICLR 2026 · Tech Insight Report

ICLR 2026 — 14th International Conference on Learning Representations

Rio de Janeiro, Brazil · April 2026

A read of ICLR 2026 through one lens: as AI shifts from single models to tool-using agents, the field's attention is moving from chasing benchmark scores to making agents reliable — so they behave well over long, messy, real-world tasks. These are the papers that show where agents break and how to make them trustworthy.

03 · Insights

Paper-by-paper tech insights

A · Why agents fail
01

Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?

Mert Cemri et al. · UC Berkeley
Goal

Find out why systems built from several cooperating LLM agents break, and sort the failures into a clear map.

Challenge

Multi-agent setups often fail, but teams had no shared way to name or diagnose what actually went wrong.

Method
  • Studied many real multi-agent runs
  • Built MAST, the first failure taxonomy (14 modes)
  • Grouped them: bad design, agents miscommunicating, weak checking/stopping
Novelty

First systematic failure map for multi-agent LLMs. Most failures come from how agents are organized — not from the model being weak.

Impact

Over 44% of failures happen during execution. Fix system design — clear roles, real coordination and verification — before adding more agents or bigger models.

[1] M. Cemri et al., “Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?,” arXiv:2503.13657, 2025.
02

LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation — Outstanding Paper

Philippe Laban et al. · Microsoft Research
Goal

Measure how well LLMs hold up across a back-and-forth conversation, not just one well-written prompt.

Challenge

Real users reveal what they want gradually, but most tests use a single fully-specified prompt — hiding this weakness.

Method
  • Ran 200,000+ simulated multi-turn chats
  • A user-simulator talks to the model across 6 task types
  • Split the score into skill vs. reliability
Novelty

Shows a large, consistent drop — about 39% — once a task is spread over several turns. Models lock onto an early guess and can’t recover.

Impact

Don’t trust single-prompt benchmarks for assistants. Build for underspecified, multi-turn use: let the model re-ground, revisit assumptions and self-correct.

[2] P. Laban et al., “LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation,” arXiv:2505.06120, 2025.
B · Reliable planning, tools & execution
03

AgentFlow: In-the-Flow Agentic System Optimization

Zhuofeng Li et al. · Stanford, UC San Diego, Texas A&M, Lambda
Goal

Train an agent to plan and use tools better while it is actually running the task — not only beforehand.

Challenge

Most tool-using agents train one policy on the whole context. That fails on long tasks where it is hard to tell which step caused success or failure.

Method
  • Splits the agent into Planner, Executor, Verifier, Generator sharing memory
  • Trains the planner live with Flow-GRPO
  • Spreads the final success/failure signal back to every step
Novelty

On-policy learning inside the multi-turn loop solves credit assignment. A 7B model beats much larger ones (incl. GPT-4o-level) on 10 benchmarks.

Impact

Strong evidence that good system design beats raw model size. Points to ‘agent-as-a-service’ built from small, trainable, modular agents.

[3] Z. Li et al., “In-the-Flow Agentic System Optimization for Effective Planning and Tool Use,” arXiv:2510.05592, 2025. (ICLR 2026 Oral)
04

TAPE: Tool-Guided Adaptive Planning & Constrained Execution

Jongwon Jeong, Jungtaek Kim, Kangwook Lee · University of Wisconsin–Madison
Goal

Make tool-using agents reliable where a single wrong move can ruin the whole task.

Challenge

Two failure types compound in strict settings: bad plans (invalid action sequences) and random slips while executing.

Method
  • Builds several candidate plans into a plan-graph
  • An external solver picks a feasible path
  • Constrained decoding removes random slips; re-plans on mismatch
Novelty

Combines multi-plan selection, constrained execution and adaptive re-planning in one loop.

Impact

+21 points success rate on hard agent benchmarks — a practical recipe where cost, latency or safety leave no room for error.

[4] J. Jeong et al., “TAPE: Tool-Guided Adaptive Planning and Constrained Execution in Language Model Agents,” arXiv:2602.19633, 2026.
05

Atomix: Transactional Tool Use for Reliable Agentic Workflows

Bardia Mohammadi et al. · (ICLR 2026)
Goal

Stop agents from leaving half-finished or duplicated real-world effects when steps fail or run in parallel.

Challenge

Tool actions (send email, write to a database) are often irreversible. Faults, speculation or multiple agents can leak partial or stale effects.

Method
  • A transactional runtime orders work in epochs
  • Commits an effect only when no earlier work remains
  • Separates reversible vs. external effects; rolls back with compensation
Novelty

Brings database transaction guarantees — atomic, isolated, recoverable — to LLM tool calls.

Impact

Task success under faults jumps from ~0–7% to ~37–57%. Enables safe parallel agents and shared-resource coordination for enterprise automation.

[5] B. Mohammadi et al., “Atomix: Timely, Transactional Tool Use for Reliable Agentic Workflows,” arXiv:2602.14849, 2026.
C · Better training & prompting
06

TROLL: Trust Regions Improve RL for LLMs

Philipp Becker et al. · (ICLR 2026 Oral)
Goal

Make reinforcement-learning fine-tuning of LLMs more stable and effective.

Challenge

The standard ‘PPO clipping’ trick is a rough shortcut: it kills gradients and collapses exploration, so training is unstable and fussy to tune.

Method
  • Replaces clipping with a proper trust-region projection
  • Enforces a principled per-token limit on change
  • Keeps gradients alive even at the boundary
Novelty

A principled objective (not a heuristic) that preserves entropy, so the model keeps exploring.

Impact

Faster, more stable training and better reasoning/code results. Trade-off: harder to implement (needs a convex layer and implicit differentiation).

[6] P. Becker et al., “TROLL: Trust Regions Improve Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models,” arXiv:2510.03817, 2025.
07

GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform RL

Lakshya A Agrawal et al. · UC Berkeley
Goal

Improve an AI system by rewriting its prompts instead of retraining its weights.

Challenge

RL methods like GRPO need thousands of expensive rollouts to adapt to a new task.

Method
  • Runs the system and reads its own traces in plain English
  • Diagnoses mistakes, proposes and tests prompt edits
  • Keeps the best ideas from a Pareto frontier of attempts
Novelty

Uses natural-language self-reflection to learn high-level rules — not just numeric rewards.

Impact

Beats GRPO by up to 20% while using up to 35× fewer rollouts — a cheap, fast alternative to fine-tuning for adapting models per domain.

[7] L. A. Agrawal et al., “GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning,” arXiv:2507.19457, 2025. (ICLR 2026 Oral)
08

SPRIG: System Prompt Optimization

Lechen Zhang et al. · U. Michigan, UIUC, UIC, LG AI Research
Goal

Automatically find a strong general-purpose system prompt that helps across many tasks.

Challenge

System prompts are usually hand-written. Good ones are hard to discover and rarely transfer.

Method
  • An edit-based genetic search over prompt components
  • Builds prompts from reusable building blocks
  • Keeps the versions that score best over 47 tasks
Novelty

Optimizes the system prompt (general instructions) rather than tuning a prompt per task.

Impact

One optimized system prompt matches per-task tuning; combining both helps more. Cheap gains with no retraining — handy per domain or region.

[8] L. Zhang et al., “SPRIG: Improving Large Language Model Performance by System Prompt Optimization,” arXiv:2410.14826, 2024.
D · Safety, constraints & security
09

SafeDPO: Preference Optimization with Enhanced Safety

Geon-Hyeong Kim et al. · LG AI Research
Goal

Align a model to be both helpful and safe in one simple training step.

Challenge

Safety alignment (safe-RLHF) usually needs separate reward and cost models plus online sampling — complex and unstable.

Method
  • Rewrites the safety-constrained goal into one closed-form loss
  • Uses only preference data plus a safety label
  • No reward model, no cost model, no online sampling
Novelty

Enforces safety at the objective level, in a single offline stage.

Impact

Competitive safety-vs-helpfulness trade-off with far less machinery — a lightweight, practical path to safe alignment.

[9] G.-H. Kim et al., “SafeDPO: A Simple Approach to Direct Preference Optimization with Enhanced Safety,” arXiv:2505.20065, 2025. (ICLR 2026 Oral)
10

Learning with Hard Constraints (ProbHardE2E)

Utkarsh et al. · MIT
Goal

Make neural models obey hard rules (physical or operational limits) while also reporting how uncertain they are.

Challenge

Standard models don’t guarantee constraints. Adding them afterward hurts quality or is unstable at scale.

Method
  • Adds a differentiable projection layer inside the network
  • Constraints are learned end-to-end, not bolted on after
  • Frames prediction probabilistically for uncertainty
Novelty

Builds feasibility into the model’s internal representation rather than filtering outputs after the fact.

Impact

Reliable, rule-respecting predictions that also say how confident they are — valuable for forecasting and safety-critical control.

[10] Utkarsh et al., “End-to-End Probabilistic Framework for Learning with Hard Constraints,” arXiv:2506.07003, 2025.
11

Mind the Gap: Agentic Vulnerabilities (AgentSeer)

Ilham Wicaksono et al. · (ICLR 2026 Workshop)
Goal

Evaluate the security of agents at the level of their actions, not just the raw model.

Challenge

Testing the model alone underestimates risk. Agents gain new attack surfaces from tool-calling, memory and multi-step reasoning.

Method
  • AgentSeer breaks a run into action graphs and component graphs
  • Pinpoints the risky individual actions
  • Hardens system prompts with a replay-based loop
Novelty

Action-level observability reveals ‘agentic-only’ weaknesses invisible at the model level (tool-calling 24–60% higher attack success).

Impact

Cut jailbreak success from ~45% to ~8%. Model-level checks aren’t enough — agent products need action-level red-teaming and prompt governance.

[11] I. Wicaksono et al., “Mind the Gap: Evaluating Model- and Agentic-Level Vulnerabilities in LLMs with Action Graphs,” arXiv:2509.04802, 2025.
12

Asymmetric Goal Drift in Coding Agents

Magnus Saebo et al. · (ICLR 2026 Workshop)
Goal

Test whether coding agents quietly stop following their instructions over a long task.

Challenge

An agent may obey at first but ‘drift’ from its system prompt as work piles up — especially when the rule clashes with its own strong values.

Method
  • Used the OpenCode agent on multi-step coding tasks
  • Added constraints on privacy, security and efficiency
  • Watched for violations over long runs
Novelty

Finds asymmetric drift: models break rules more when the rule opposes values they hold strongly; repo comments can even override the system prompt.

Impact

Initial compliance checks aren’t enough. Coding / DevOps agents need long-horizon drift monitoring and repo-level, environment-aware security controls.

[12] M. Saebo et al., “Asymmetric Goal Drift in Coding Agents Under Value Conflict,” arXiv:2603.03456, 2026.
04 · Conclusions

Synthesis across the papers

Insights

  • Reliability — not peak accuracy — is the new scoreboard for agents.
  • Most agent failures come from system design and coordination, not weak models.
  • Small, well-designed modular agents can beat much larger single models.

Vision

  • Benchmarks shift from scoring models to scoring whole agent pipelines.
  • Training moves in-loop (live) and safety/constraints move into the objective.
  • Tool use gets database-style guarantees; prompts get optimized automatically.

Implications for us

  • Prioritize agent system design, verification and execution reliability.
  • Add action-level red-teaming and long-horizon drift monitoring to agent products.
  • Prefer cheap adaptation (reflective prompts, optimized system prompts) over retraining.
